analysis.one_liner: Creates ethics-advice and investigative offices inside the Supreme Court to handle complaints against justices.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 10 Democratic cosponsors on February 25, 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up two new offices inside the Supreme Court. One would advise justices and their spouses on ethics rules covering gifts, financial disclosure, conflicts of interest, recusal, and political activity, and require them to take ethics training twice a year. The other would investigate formal ethics complaints against justices, with power to subpoena witnesses and documents, and report findings and recommendations — including to Congress and, when a complaint involves possible crimes, to the Attorney General. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has seen no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who depend on a court whose rulings bind everyone else. The bill gives the public, through their congressional leaders, a real channel for the first time to file complaints about justices' conduct and get an investigation with subpoena power — complaints filed by congressional leaders, reviewed within 60 days, with reports shared with the House and Senate Judiciary Committees. It also benefits justices themselves in a small way: for the first time they would have professional ethics counsel to consult before accepting gifts or handling conflicts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary people seeking an accountable Court

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Office of Investigative Counsel inside the Supreme Court to review and investigate ethics complaints against justices arising from their actions or those of their spouses and dependents.
Gives the Chief Investigative Counsel power to issue subpoenas for testimony and documents, enforceable in federal court with contempt penalties for noncompliance.

Requires a review of every complaint within 60 days and, if warranted, a full investigation with written findings and recommendations (such as recusal or divestiture) delivered to the Chief Justice — or to the most senior associate justice if the Chief Justice himself is the subject.

Creates an Office of Ethics Counsel to advise justices and their spouses on gifts, financial disclosure, conflicts of interest, recusal, and political activity, and requires justices to take ethics training twice a year.
Requires annual public-facing reports to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees on how much ethics advice was sought, on what topics, and how often it was not followed.
Requires the investigative office to report to the Attorney General whenever it has reasonable grounds to believe a federal crime has occurred.

analysis.who_pays: Supreme Court justices, who would face formal investigation of their conduct for the first time, including scrutiny of their spouses' and dependents' activities, with subpoena power behind it. Taxpayers would fund the new offices (counsel salaries of at least $225,000 and $180,000 a year, respectively). Congressional leaders who misuse the complaint process could waste investigative resources.

drawbacks.text: Only congressional leaders — committee chairs and ranking members, Senate and House party leaders, and the Speaker — may file ethics complaints; ordinary citizens cannot file directly.

The Chief Justice appoints the chief ethics and investigative counsels and can remove them only for cause, so the watchdog is created and kept by the very institution it watches, and the Chief Justice may release investigation reports to the public solely at his own discretion.

The bill includes a severability clause anticipating that a court could strike parts of it as unconstitutional, an acknowledgment that subjecting the Supreme Court to congressionally created investigative machinery raises separation-of-powers questions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The need is real: the Supreme Court adopted a Code of Conduct in 2023 but has no enforcement office to investigate complaints, unlike every other federal court. This bill fills that gap, though the design has genuine weaknesses — the counsels are appointed by the Chief Justice, only congressional leaders can trigger investigations, and publication of findings is discretionary — so the accountability it creates depends heavily on the officeholders themselves. The cost to taxpayers is modest; the main cost is borne by the justices' own insulation from scrutiny, which is the point.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and the committee has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Daniel Goldman (D-NY) introduced the Supreme Court Ethics and Investigations Act on February 25, 2026.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which is the only action recorded so far.
Ten Democratic members — including Jerrold Nadler, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Raja Krishnamoorthi — cosponsored the bill; no Republicans are listed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo: Supreme Court justices remain the only judges in the federal system with no independent office to investigate ethics complaints against them, and no committee has taken up the bill to change that.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Justices, who keep the status quo

against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on February 25, 2026 with no hearing, markup, or vote recorded since.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 original supporters are Democrats; no Republican cosponsors are listed, and the bill now sits with a Republican-controlled committee that has not acted.

industries.note: The bill would end the justices' unique position as the only federal judges without an investigative office for ethics complaints, exposing them and their households to subpoena-backed scrutiny. Justices' institutional interest in avoiding outside investigation runs directly against the public's interest in an accountable Court.

analysis.trajectory: Very unlikely to advance this Congress. A Democratic-only ethics bill targeting the Supreme Court sits in a committee run by the Republican majority with no action since referral; bills at this stage without committee action, hearings, or minority-party support overwhelmingly die when the session ends.
